title: The yellow in autumn leaves was there all summer, hidden under the green

cover.alt: Maple leaves in autumn colours, red, orange and yellow, lying together.

body: Leaves are packed with chlorophyll, the green pigment that captures sunlight, and there is so much of it that it masks the yellow and orange **carotenoids** sitting beside it all season. In late summer, shorter days and cooler temperatures tell the tree to stop making chlorophyll and to pull nutrients back out of the leaf, and as the green breaks down the carotenoids are finally revealed. Reds and purples are different: **anthocyanins** are made freshly in autumn from sugars trapped in the leaf, brightest when bright, cool days are followed by chilly but frost-free nights. Finally a layer of cork cells forms at the base of the stalk and the leaf lets go.

slides.heading: Already there, or made in autumn?
slides.explanation: Carotenoids sit in the leaf all summer under the chlorophyll. Anthocyanins are built in autumn from sugars as phosphate drains out of the leaf.

steps.label: A cork layer forms and the leaf drops

left.label: Yellow and orange
left.text: Carotenoids, present all year and unmasked when chlorophyll breaks down. Hickory, ash, aspen, birch and sycamore turn these colours.

right.label: Red and purple
right.text: Anthocyanins, made in autumn from trapped sugars in bright light. Maples, oaks, sweetgum and dogwood can blaze red.

slides.heading: About 1 in 10 temperate tree species make red anthocyanins
slides.note: In northern New England the share rises to as much as 70%

slides.label: tree species in North America, against 51 in Western Europe
slides.text: One reason the autumn display in New England is so famously varied.

slides.question: Which weather gives the brightest reds?
slides.explanation: Bright light drives anthocyanin production from sugars trapped in the leaf, and cool nights keep those sugars there. The recipe: bright, cool days and chilly but not freezing nights.
